title: Overview and justification
body:
This short course is about academic presentations: what they are and how one is put together. By the end you will be able to explain what an academic presentation is and why it is used, describe how a presentation is planned and structured, and identify effective visual aids and the common errors to avoid.

These are not abstract skills. Presentations are a common form of assessment across subjects, and they build the communication skills that employers look for. Knowing what a presentation is, and how to build one, changes how you prepare and the marks your work earns.

title: Learning outcomes
body: By the end of this course, you will be able to:

_items.text: explain what an academic presentation is and why it is used
describe how a presentation is planned and structured
identify the features of effective visual aids and the common errors to avoid.

title: In real academic practice
body: Presenting is a skill academic study asks of you again and again. Seminars, poster sessions, group projects and vivas all ask you to speak to an audience and make a point clearly. The same skill is prized at work, where employers value graduates who can communicate well. Build the foundations now and they carry into every module of your degree, and into professional life beyond it.

title: Signpost
body: The course has three short lessons. First, what a presentation is: the form and why it is used. Second, planning and structuring a presentation: how one is put together, from the brief to a clear shape. Third, designing visual aids and avoiding common errors: making slides that help rather than hinder. Work through them in order; each builds on the one before.

title: Course instructions
body:
Start and finish with a confidence check. Before the lessons, you'll rate how confident you feel about each part of this topic. You'll rate the same statements again at the end, so you can see what has changed. Your ratings are yours: they aren't marked and no one else sees them.

The activities in the lessons are for practice. Questions, examples and reflective prompts are there to help you think, and they don't count towards passing. Reflective prompts are private and optional.

The test at the end is the one that counts. To complete the course you need to take the final test and score at least 70%. You can retake it.

title: Orientation
body: Sooner or later your course will ask you to give a presentation. It can feel daunting if you are not sure what a presentation actually is, or why you are being asked to give one. A presentation is not just reading information aloud. This lesson looks at what an academic presentation is, and why tutors use it, so the task stops feeling vague and starts being something you can prepare for.

title: Orientation: at this level
body: You are early in your studies, and giving a presentation for assessment may be new. At this stage you are not expected to present like a polished professional. The aim is to understand what a presentation is and why it is used, so you can recognise what is being asked of you and build from there.

title: Learning outcomes
body: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:

_items.text: explain what an academic presentation is as a form of assessment
give an example of a transferable skill that presenting builds
recognise a type of presentation used for assessment in {{context}}.

title: Concept: definition
body:
An academic presentation is a spoken piece of work, usually supported by visual aids, in which you communicate an argument or set of findings to an audience. It is a form of assessment: your tutor is marking how clearly you understand your topic and how well you can convey it. In this way a presentation develops your academic voice, much as an essay does, but out loud and to a live audience.

Presentations come in several forms, such as an individual talk, a poster, or a group presentation. They also build transferable skills, above all clear communication, which employers value highly. This lesson is about what a presentation is and why it is used; the lessons that follow are about how you plan, structure and design one.

title: Explore the concept
body: One key term at the heart of this lesson. Select the card to reveal more each time.
instruction: Select the card to reveal the definition, an example and related terms.
definition: A spoken piece of assessed work in which you communicate an argument or findings to an audience, usually with visual aids.
extendedDefinition: An academic presentation is marked like other work. It develops your academic voice out loud, and builds communication skills that carry beyond your degree.
example: A student gives a ten-minute talk with slides, setting out a question, the evidence, and a conclusion for the class and tutor.

title: Worked example
body:
Consider two students given the same brief: a ten-minute presentation on a topic from their module.

{{learner-a}} treats the task as reading out information. {{learner-a}} copies notes onto slides and plans to read them aloud, line by line, to get through the material. The topic is covered, but the audience is left to follow dense slides while {{learner-a}} reads. The presentation is really a document read out, not a talk. This misses what a presentation is for.

{{learner-b}} treats the task as communicating a point to an audience. {{learner-b}} works out one clear message, chooses what the audience needs to hear, and uses the slides to support the spoken argument rather than to carry it. The talk has a shape and a purpose. This is what an academic presentation is: a spoken argument, made clearly to listeners.

Both students had the same brief. Only {{learner-b}} understood that a presentation is communication to an audience, not a document read aloud.

title: Orientation
body: In the last lesson you saw what a presentation is: communication of a point to an audience. This lesson is about how you put one together. A good presentation does not happen by opening slide software and typing. It is planned first, then given a clear shape, so the audience can follow it from start to finish.

title: Orientation: at this level
body: You are not expected to produce a flawless, polished talk yet. The aim here is to understand the steps involved in preparing a presentation, and the simple three-part structure that most presentations share, so you have a reliable way to start.

title: Learning outcomes
body: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:

_items.text: describe the main steps in preparing a presentation
identify the three parts of a presentation's structure: introduction, main body and conclusion
choose an appropriate planning or structuring move for a presentation in {{context}}.

title: Concept: definition
body:
Preparing a presentation works best as a series of steps. First, read the brief and the marking criteria closely, so you know what is being asked. Next, research your topic and gather what you need. Then plan the presentation: decide your main message and the order of your points. After that, design your visual aids to support those points. Finally, practise, so the timing and delivery settle.

Planning is also where you set the structure. Most presentations share a simple three-part shape: an introduction that tells the audience what is coming, a main body that develops the points in a logical order, and a conclusion that draws them together. This structure is not a straitjacket, but it gives the audience a path to follow.

title: Explore the concept
body: The five stages of preparing a presentation, in order. Select each stage to reveal what it involves.
instruction: Select each stage in turn to see what it involves.

_items.title: Understand the brief
_items.body: Read the task and the marking criteria closely. Work out what kind of presentation it is, how long it should be, and what is being assessed.

_items.title: Research
_items.body: Gather and read what you need on the topic. Decide which material actually earns a place in the talk.

_items.title: Plan and structure
_items.body: Decide your one main message and the order of your points. Set the shape: introduction, main body, conclusion.

_items.title: Design visual aids
_items.body: Make slides or other aids that support your spoken points, rather than carry all the words themselves.

_items.title: Practise
_items.body: Rehearse the talk so the timing settles and the delivery feels steadier. Adjust anything that runs long.

title: Worked example
body:
Two students prepare the same ten-minute presentation.

{{learner-a}} opens the slide software straight away and starts making slides. Points go in as they come to mind, with no clear order and no single message. The result is a set of slides that jump about, and a talk the audience cannot follow. {{learner-a}} skipped the planning, so the presentation has no shape.

{{learner-b}} plans first. {{learner-b}} reads the brief, researches the topic, then decides on one main message and the order of points. Only then are the slides made. The talk opens with an introduction, develops its points in the main body, and ends with a conclusion. {{learner-b}} practises it once to check the timing. The audience can follow it easily.

Both had the same time to prepare. Only {{learner-b}} planned and structured the presentation before building the slides.

title: Planning moves
body: These moves turn a blank start into a planned, structured presentation. Try them before you make any slides.
instruction: Tick each item once you have done it.

_items.text: Have I read the brief and marking criteria before starting?
Have I decided the one main message of my presentation?
Have I chosen the order my points should come in?
Have I planned an introduction that tells the audience what is coming?
Have I planned a conclusion that draws the points together?
Have I planned to practise the talk before giving it?

_items.text: Open the slide software and add points as they come to mind.

_items.text: Work through steps: understand the brief, research, plan, design, then practise.
_items.feedback: Yes. Preparing in these steps gives the presentation a clear shape.

_items.text: Write the whole talk out and read it aloud from the page.
_items.feedback: Reading a script aloud is not the same as planning and structuring a talk.

_items.text: Make as many slides as possible to fill the time.
_items.feedback: Filling time with slides is not preparation; planning the message and shape is.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Preparing a presentation in steps, from the brief through to practice, gives it shape.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Look for the option that works through planning steps before building slides.
_incorrect.final: Preparing a presentation means working through steps: understand the brief, research, plan, design, then practise. Starting with slides, reading a script or padding the time all skip the planning.

title: Formative check: the three-part structure
displayTitle: A presentation's main body comes between which two parts of its structure?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: The main body of a presentation comes between which two parts?

_items.text: Between the introduction and the conclusion.
_items.feedback: Yes. The usual shape is introduction, then main body, then conclusion.

_items.text: Between the conclusion and the references.
_items.feedback: The main body comes before the conclusion, not after it.

_items.text: Between two sets of slides with no introduction.
_items.feedback: A presentation opens with an introduction, not straight into the body.

_items.text: Between the research and the brief.
_items.feedback: Research and the brief are preparation steps, not parts of the talk's structure.

_feedback.correct: That's right. The main body sits between the introduction and the conclusion.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Think about the usual order: what comes first, and what comes last?
_incorrect.final: The main body sits between the introduction, which opens the talk, and the conclusion, which draws it together. The other options confuse the structure with preparation steps or slides.

title: Formative check: a planning move
displayTitle: You are planning a presentation in {{context}} and have gathered more material than will fit. Which is the better planning move?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Which is the better planning move when you have too much material?

_items.text: Decide the one main message and keep only the points that serve it.
_items.feedback: Yes. Choosing a main message and cutting to it is a sound planning move in {{context}}.

_items.text: Put every point in so none of your research is wasted.
_items.feedback: Cramming in everything leaves the audience with no clear message to follow.

_items.text: Add more slides so the extra material has somewhere to go.
_items.feedback: More slides do not solve the problem; a clear message and selection do.

_items.text: Leave out the introduction to save time for the content.
_items.feedback: Dropping the introduction removes the signpost the audience needs.

_feedback.correct: That's right. In {{context}}, choosing one main message and keeping only what serves it is the sound move.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Look for the option that selects material around a clear message.
_incorrect.final: The better move is to decide the one main message and keep only the points that serve it. Cramming in everything, adding slides or dropping the introduction all weaken the talk.

title: Orientation
body: You know what a presentation is, and how to plan and structure one. This lesson is about the visual aids, usually slides, and the common errors that trip people up. Slides can help an audience follow you, or they can get in the way. The difference is in how they are designed.

title: Orientation: at this level
body: You are not expected to produce designer-quality slides. The aim is to recognise what makes a visual aid effective, to tell a clear slide from an overloaded one, and to know the common errors so you can avoid them.

title: Learning outcomes
body: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:

_items.text: identify the features of an effective visual aid
tell an effective slide apart from an overloaded one
recognise a common presentation error in {{context}} and the move that avoids it.

title: Concept: definition
body:
A visual aid is there to support what you say, not to replace it. An effective slide is clear and uncluttered: a few words or one image that back up your spoken point, so the audience listens to you rather than reading a wall of text. The presentation is about your argument and your delivery; the slides serve them.

Common errors follow from forgetting this. Overloading slides with text, then reading them out, is the most frequent. Others include slides that are hard to read, visual aids that distract rather than help, and letting the talk run over time. Knowing these errors in advance is the simplest way to avoid them.

title: Explore the concept
body: Four principles for visual aids that help rather than hinder. Review each card.
instruction: Read through the cards below.

_items.title: Support, don't replace
_items.subtitle: The golden rule
_items.text: Slides back up your spoken point. The talk is your argument; the slides serve it, so the audience listens to you.

_items.title: Keep it simple
_items.subtitle: Less is more
_items.text: A few words or one clear image per slide. Avoid dense paragraphs the audience has to read while you speak.

_items.title: Make it readable
_items.subtitle: From the back row
_items.text: Large text, strong contrast and clear images. If it cannot be read from the back of the room, it is too small.

_items.title: Stay relevant
_items.subtitle: Help, don't distract
_items.text: Every visual should earn its place by helping the point. Cut decoration and animation that pulls attention away.

title: Worked example
body:
Two students design slides for the same presentation.

{{learner-a}} fills each slide with full paragraphs of text, then reads them out word for word. The slides are crowded and hard to read from the back. The audience reads ahead and stops listening, and {{learner-a}} runs over time. The slides have taken over the talk. This is the most common presentation error: the overloaded, read-aloud slide.

{{learner-b}} puts only a few words or one image on each slide, enough to cue the point, and speaks around them. The slides are easy to read and support what {{learner-b}} says rather than repeating it. The audience listens, and the talk keeps to time. The slides help the argument instead of carrying it.

Both had the same content. Only {{learner-b}} designed slides that support the talk rather than crowd it out.

title: Checking your slides
body: Use these questions to check your visual aids and avoid the common errors. Try them on your next set of slides.
instruction: Tick each item once you have checked it.

_items.text: Does each slide support a spoken point, rather than carry all the words?
Could I read every slide from the back of the room?
Have I cut any slide that is a wall of text?
Have I removed decoration or animation that distracts?
Am I speaking around the slides, not reading them aloud?
Have I checked the talk keeps to the time allowed?

title: Formative check: effective visual aids
displayTitle: Which of these best describes an effective visual aid?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Which option best describes an effective visual aid?

_items.text: A slide packed with full paragraphs so nothing is left out.
_items.feedback: A packed slide is the overloaded error; it makes the audience read instead of listen.

_items.text: A clear, uncluttered slide that supports your spoken point.
_items.feedback: Yes. An effective visual aid is clear and supports what you say.

_items.text: A slide with as much animation as possible to hold attention.
_items.feedback: Animation for its own sake distracts rather than helps.

_items.text: A slide you read out word for word to the audience.
_items.feedback: Reading a slide aloud is the common error, not effective design.

_feedback.correct: That's right. An effective visual aid is clear, uncluttered and supports your spoken point.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Look for the option about a clear slide that supports what you say.
_incorrect.final: An effective visual aid is clear and uncluttered and supports your spoken point. Packed text, excess animation and reading slides aloud are all common errors.

title: Formative check: effective versus overloaded
displayTitle: In the worked example, what made the stronger student's slides better than the weaker student's?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: What made the stronger student's slides better?

_items.text: They used a few words or one image to support the point, not full paragraphs.
_items.feedback: Yes. Spare slides that support the talk are the effective design.

_items.text: They had more slides than the weaker student's.
_items.feedback: The number of slides was not what made the difference.

_items.text: They used brighter colours on every slide.
_items.feedback: Colour alone does not make a slide effective; clarity and support do.

_items.text: They repeated the spoken words exactly on each slide.
_items.feedback: Repeating the words on the slide is the overloaded error.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Spare slides that support the spoken point, rather than carry it, are the better design.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Look for what the stronger student's slides did with text and images.
_incorrect.final: The stronger student's slides used a few words or one image to support the point. More slides, brighter colours or repeated text do not make a slide effective.

title: Formative check: avoiding a common error
displayTitle: While preparing a presentation in {{context}}, you notice your slides are full of text you plan to read out. Which move avoids the common error?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Which move avoids the common error of overloaded, read-aloud slides?

_items.text: Cut the text to a few key words and speak around them instead.
_items.feedback: Yes. Trimming the text and speaking around it avoids the overloaded-slide error in {{context}}.

_items.text: Add even more detail so nothing important is missed.
_items.feedback: More detail makes the overloaded-slide error worse, not better.

_items.text: Make the font smaller so all the text fits on one slide.
_items.feedback: Smaller text makes the slide harder to read; it does not fix the problem.

_items.text: Read the slides faster so you keep to time.
_items.feedback: Reading faster does not fix overloaded slides; cutting the text does.

_feedback.correct: That's right. In {{context}}, cutting the text and speaking around it avoids the overloaded-slide error.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Look for the move that reduces the text and shifts it to your spoken delivery.
_incorrect.final: Cutting the text to a few key words and speaking around them avoids the error. Adding detail, shrinking the font or reading faster all keep the overloaded slide.

title: Reflective prompt
body: Think of a set of slides you have seen that were hard to follow. What went wrong with them? What is one thing you will do differently with your own slides?
instruction: Write a few sentences for yourself. This is not marked, and there are no right answers.

title: Summary
body: Visual aids are there to support what you say, not to replace it. An effective slide is clear and uncluttered; the common errors, above all the overloaded slide read aloud, follow from forgetting that. You can now identify the features of an effective visual aid, tell a clear slide from an overloaded one, and recognise a common error and the move that avoids it. With what a presentation is, how to plan and structure one, and how to design its slides, you have the foundations to build a presentation of your own.

What is an academic presentation, mainly?

body: Which of these is a transferable skill that giving presentations builds?

body: Which order best describes preparing a presentation?

body: What are the three parts of a presentation's usual structure, in order?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: What are the three parts of a presentation's structure, in order?

_items.text: Introduction, main body, conclusion.
_items.feedback: Yes. That is the usual three-part shape.

_items.text: Conclusion, introduction, main body.
_items.feedback: The introduction comes first, not the conclusion.

_items.text: References, slides, questions.
_items.feedback: These are not the three structural parts of the talk.

_items.text: Research, planning, practice.
_items.feedback: These are preparation steps, not the parts of the talk's structure.

_feedback.correct: That's right. The usual structure is introduction, main body, then conclusion.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Think about how a talk opens, develops and closes.

body: Which of these describes an effective visual aid?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Which describes an effective visual aid?

_items.text: A clear, uncluttered slide that supports your spoken point.
_items.feedback: Yes. Effective slides are clear and support the talk.

_items.text: A slide filled with full paragraphs to read aloud.
_items.feedback: A packed, read-aloud slide is the common error.

_items.text: A slide with the smallest font that fits the text.
_items.feedback: Tiny text makes a slide hard to read; it is not effective.

_items.text: A slide crowded with animation to hold attention.
_items.feedback: Excess animation distracts rather than helps.

_feedback.correct: That's right. An effective visual aid is clear and supports your spoken point.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Think about a slide that helps the audience listen to you.

body: Your slides are full of text you plan to read out. Which move avoids this common error?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Which move avoids the overloaded, read-aloud slide?

_items.text: Cut the text to a few key words and speak around them.
_items.feedback: Yes. Trimming the text and speaking around it avoids the error.

_items.text: Add more text so nothing is left out.
_items.feedback: More text makes the overloaded slide worse.

_items.text: Shrink the font so all the text fits.
_items.feedback: Smaller text does not fix an overloaded slide.

_items.text: Read the slides faster to keep to time.
_items.feedback: Reading faster does not fix overloaded slides.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Cut the text to a few key words and speak around them.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Think about reducing the text and shifting it to your delivery.

title: Course summary
body: You have reached the end of the course. A presentation is no longer a daunting unknown: it is a form of work you understand and can prepare for. You can explain what an academic presentation is and why it is used, a spoken argument made to an audience and assessed. You can describe how one is planned and structured, from the brief through to an introduction, main body and conclusion. And you can identify effective visual aids and the common errors to avoid. Look back at the confidence check: comparing where you started with where you are now shows how far this has moved.

title: In real academic practice
body: From here, presenting is something you practise in many modules. Each seminar talk, each poster, each group presentation puts these foundations to work. It is also what professional life rewards: the ability to communicate an idea clearly to an audience travels well beyond your degree, and is among the skills employers ask for most.

title: Where this goes next
body: Two directions build on this. Going deeper: the intermediate and advanced presenting courses take you into delivering a presentation well across different formats, and into presenting with authority and collaborating in group work. Going wider: the same foundations underpin Academic Writing, Reflective Practice and Work-Based and Experiential Learning, where you put communication to work on real tasks.

title: Orientation
body: You have now looked at three things: what a presentation is, how one is planned and structured, and how its visual aids are designed. On their own they are three separate ideas. This lesson brings them together into one practice you can use.

title: Orientation: at this level
body: At this stage you are not expected to deliver a polished talk. The aim is to see presenting as one connected practice rather than three separate tasks, so it carries on into the presentations you give across your studies.

title: Learning outcomes
body: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:

_items.text: recognise how what a presentation is, how it is planned and structured, and how its visual aids are designed connect as one practice
show the three strands working together in a worked example of a student building a presentation
plan one way to build your next presentation in {{context}} as one connected practice

title: Concept: definition
body: Building a presentation is one connected practice, not three separate jobs. You start from what a presentation is, a clear message spoken to an audience. You plan and structure it so the audience can follow that message. Then you design slides that support it. One idea holds the three together: everything you do serves one clear message to your audience.

title: Concept: in practice
body: In practice, the three ideas stop being separate once you build a real presentation. You decide your message, shape the talk around it, and design slides that back it up, all in one go. The thread running through them is the audience: everything you do is there to get one clear message across to them.

title: Reflective prompt
body: Think of a presentation you will need to give soon in your studies. What is your one clear message, and how will you make the structure and slides serve it?
instruction: Write a few sentences for yourself. This is not marked, and the questions have no right answers.

title: Summary
body: Building a presentation is most useful when you treat it as one practice, not three separate jobs. You decide a clear message, structure the talk around it, and design slides that support it, all serving the same goal. It is the parts working together, towards one message for your audience, that makes a presentation land.

title: The steps as one process
body: Building a presentation runs as a sequence. Select each step to see what it involves.
instruction: Select each step.

_items.title: Message
_items.body: Decide your one clear message and who the audience is.

_items.title: Structure
_items.body: Plan and structure the talk so the audience can follow, with an introduction, body and conclusion.

_items.title: Design
_items.body: Design slides that support your message rather than replace it.

_items.title: Practise
_items.body: Practise the talk, check the timing, then give it.

title: Worked example
body: Two students have the same presentation to give. One treats it as three separate jobs, writes dense slides, and never settles on a message, so the talk has no shape. The other decides one clear message, plans a structure around it, and designs slides that support it. Over the talk, the second student carries the audience with them, because the parts worked as one practice.

title: Working with the cycle
displayTitle: Checklist: How to build a whole presentation
body: Use these questions to keep the three ideas working together as one practice.
instruction: Tick each item when you have done it.

_items.text: Do I know my one clear message and who the audience is?
Have I planned a structure the audience can follow from start to finish?
Do my slides support that message rather than carry all the words?
Have I checked for the common errors, such as the overloaded, read-aloud slide?
Have I practised the talk so it keeps to time?

displayTitle: Why is it more useful to treat building a presentation as one connected practice rather than three separate tasks?
body: Why is it more useful to treat building a presentation as one connected practice rather than three separate tasks?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Why is it more useful to treat building a presentation as one connected practice rather than three separate tasks?

_items.text: Because each part serves the same goal: getting one clear message across to your audience, so the parts support each other.
_items.feedback: Yes. One clear message to the audience is the thread that ties the three parts into one practice.

_items.text: Because doing them separately means you never have to plan the talk.
_items.feedback: Planning is one of the parts. The practice joins planning to the message and the slides.

_items.text: Because one practice means you can skip designing the slides.
_items.feedback: The slides are part of the practice. They support your message rather than being skipped.

_items.text: Because treating it as one practice takes less thought than planning each part.
_items.feedback: It is not about less thought. Seeing one goal keeps the parts pulling the same way.

_feedback.correct: That's right. One clear message to the audience holds what a presentation is, how you plan it, and how you design the slides into one practice.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Think about what the three parts have in common, and what they are all working towards.

displayTitle: A student works out one clear message, plans an introduction, main body and conclusion around it, and builds slides that support it. The talk lands well. What does this show?
body: A student works out one clear message, plans an introduction, main body and conclusion around it, and builds slides that support it. The talk lands well. What does this show?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: A student works out one clear message, plans an introduction, main body and conclusion around it, and builds slides that support it. The talk lands well. What does this show?

_items.text: That building a presentation works as one practice: the message, the structure and the slides all pulled the same way.
_items.feedback: Yes. The three parts worked together towards one clear message, which is the whole practice.

_items.text: That the slides were the only thing that mattered.
_items.feedback: The slides helped, but only because they supported a clear message and a sound structure.

_items.text: That the student was lucky, and planning made no difference.
_items.feedback: Planning shaped the talk. The parts working together are what made it land.

_items.text: That a clear message on its own is enough, without structure or slides.
_items.feedback: The message mattered, but the structure and slides carried it. All three worked together.

_feedback.correct: That's right. The message, the structure and the slides worked together, which is building a presentation as one practice.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Look at what the student did across the message, the structure and the slides.

displayTitle: You have a presentation to give in {{context}} this term. Which plan best treats building it as one connected practice?
body: You have a presentation to give in {{context}} this term. Which plan best treats building it as one connected practice?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: You have a presentation to give in your subject this term. Which plan best treats building it as one connected practice?

_items.text: Decide your one clear message, plan a structure around it, then design slides that support it, and practise.
_items.feedback: Yes. That runs the whole practice, with every part serving one clear message to the audience.

_items.text: Open the slide software and add points as they come to mind.
_items.feedback: That skips the message and the structure. The slides end up carrying a talk with no shape.

_items.text: Write out the whole talk and read it from the page.
_items.feedback: Reading it out is not presenting to an audience. The practice plans a message and supports it with slides.

_items.text: Make as many detailed slides as possible to fill the time.
_items.feedback: More slides is not the goal. The parts should serve one clear message, not fill time.

_feedback.correct: That's right. A clear message, a sound structure and supporting slides, then practice, is building a presentation as one practice.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Think about which plan keeps the message, the structure and the slides working together.

title: Summative item 7 (tests co4)
displayTitle: What best describes building a presentation as one connected practice?
body: What best describes building a presentation as one connected practice?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: What best describes building a presentation as one connected practice?

_items.text: The message, the structure and the slides all serve one clear message to the audience.
_items.feedback: Yes. One clear message holds the three parts together.

_items.text: Making as many slides as possible so no material is left out.
_items.feedback: More slides is not the aim. The parts should serve one clear message.

_items.text: Planning the talk but leaving the slides until there is no time to design them.
_items.feedback: The slides are part of the practice. They need designing to support the message.

_items.text: Reading the written talk aloud so nothing is forgotten.
_items.feedback: Reading it out is not presenting. A presentation is a clear message spoken to an audience.

_feedback.correct: Correct.

title: Summative item 8 (tests co4)
displayTitle: A student decides one message, structures the talk around it, designs slides that support it, and practises. What does this show?
body: A student decides one message, structures the talk around it, designs slides that support it, and practises. What does this show?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: A student decides one message, structures the talk around it, designs slides that support it, and practises. What does this show?

_items.text: The three parts worked together as one practice, serving one clear message.
_items.feedback: Yes. The message, the structure and the slides all pulled the same way.

_items.text: That the slides alone decided whether the talk worked.
